title: On Guerrilla Warfare
author: Mao Zedong
context: First published in 1937 during the Second Sino-Japanese War while Mao Zedong was based in Yan'an, this seminal treatise outlines the military and political doctrine of protracted guerrilla warfare. Mao establishes that guerrilla warfare is not merely a military tactic, but a political struggle of the masses against a foreign invader or oppressive ruling class, requiring deep integration with the population.
relatesToToday: Mao's famous formulation that 'the people are like water, and the guerrilla is like a fish who swims in it' remains a cornerstone of asymmetric warfare and anti-colonial resistance theory. It highlights that political mobilization, popular support, and military discipline are inseparable when weaker forces resist technologically superior invading armies.
keyTakeaways: Guerrilla warfare is fundamentally a political instrument; victory depends on winning the active support, trust, and mobilization of the civilian population.
Guerrilla operations must coordinate closely with regular armed forces, acting as a supportive shield during early defensive stages and preparing to transition into conventional counter-offensives.
Tactical flexibility, surprise attacks, mobility, and strict political discipline (respecting civilian rights and property) are essential to sustain long-term resistance.
